travelAdvisory.summary:
Reissued after periodic review with minor edits. 
Exercise normal precautions in Portugal.
Read the country information page for additional information on travel to Portugal.  
If you decide to travel to Portugal:  

Enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive travel alerts and make it easier to locate you in an emergency.

healthcare.costForTourists: System: Universal (Serviço Nacional de Saúde / SNS) Quality: ★★★★☆ (4/5) Good healthcare system with modern facilities, particularly in Lisbon, Porto, and the Algarve. English is commonly spoken in tourist areas and private healthcare. Public healthcare is accessible but can have longer wait times. Many private hospitals and clinics cater to tourists. 💡 Medical Tourism Portugal is emerging as a medical tourism destination for dental work, cosmetic surgery, and wellness retreats, combining quality healthcare with affordable living costs.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Access: very_easy Hours: Most pharmacies open 9am-7pm weekdays, with reduced hours on weekends. In every area, one pharmacy stays open 24/7 or for extended hours — look for the green cross sign or ask any pharmacy for the nearest 'farmácia de serviço/noturno' (on-duty pharmacy). Prescription rules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require validation by a Portuguese doctor. Many medications that are OTC in some countries require prescriptions here. 💡 Tips Pharmacies (farmácia) are very accessible and pharmacists are helpful. Many medications require a prescription. Portugal has a strong pharmacy culture — pharmacists can advise on minor ailments and some medications are available without prescription.

Private hospitals and clinics are excellent but require payment or insurance guarantee upfront. vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers from most countries.

water.notes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Portugal, though many people prefer the taste of bottled water (especially in the Algarve).

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Portuguese cuisine is delicious and generally safe. Bacalhau (salted cod) is a staple — safe from reputable restaurants. Fresh seafood, sardines, and grilled fish are excellent and safe. Pastéis de nata (egg tarts) from bakeries are safe. Be cautious with mayonnaise-based salads in hot weather.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for short stays, but strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC.
travelInsurance.tips: INEM (national emergency service) provides free emergency medical care. Private hospitals and clinics are excellent but require payment or insurance guarantee upfront. Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is recommended.

Public healthcare is accessible but can have longer wait times. Many private hospitals and clinics cater to tourists.

medications.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require validation by a Portuguese doctor. Many medications that are OTC in some countries require prescriptions here.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in Portugal. Some codeine products may be restricted.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, methylphenidate)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A Portuguese prescription or special authorization is required.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring a prescription. Portugal has strict regulations.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal in Portugal for specific conditions. THC/cannabis products remain heavily restricted.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter and prescription (ideally in Portuguese or English) for all medications. Bring sufficient supply in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry prescription documentation. EU citizens should carry the EHIC/GHIC card.
medications.generalAdvice: Portugal decriminalized personal use of all drugs in 2001 — possession of small amounts is treated as a public health issue, not a criminal offense. However, this applies only to Portuguese residents; tourists should not assume the same leniency. Prescription medications should be in original containers with EU Schengen certificates for controlled substances.

controlledSubstances.note: Decriminalized for personal use (up to 25g of plant material or 5g of hashish). Not legal — still confiscated, and you may be referred to a 'dissuasion commission.' Medical cannabis is legal with a Portuguese prescription. Do not bring cannabis into Portugal.
Controlled substances. EU/EEA travelers need a Schengen certificate. Non-EU travelers need a doctor's letter. Carry in original packaging with clear labeling.
Controlled under Portuguese and EU law. Schengen certificate required for EU/EEA travelers. Carry documentation and original packaging.
Controlled psychotropic substances. Requires Schengen certificate or doctor's letter. Widely prescribed in Portugal and available at local pharmacies with a prescription.

Decriminalized for personal-use quantities (e.g., cocaine up to 2g, MDMA up to 1g). Still illegal — substances are confiscated and you face administrative penalties. Trafficking remains a serious criminal offense with up to 12 years imprisonment.
Decriminalized for personal use under the same 2001 law. Fresh mushrooms exist in a gray area. Do not attempt to import.

connectivity.simOptions: Prepaid SIMs from NOS (best coverage), MEO, or Vodafone PT at airports, post offices (CTT), and phone shops. ~€10-20 for 10-25GB. eSIM via Airalo or Holafly from $5 USD.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Excellent WiFi in Lisbon, Porto, and Algarve hotels and cafes. Good coverage in most tourist areas. Free public WiFi in many city centers and plazas.
connectivity.bestOption: NOS or MEO prepaid SIM for widest national coverage. Buy at Lisbon Humberto Delgado Airport or at any CTT post office. eSIM from Airalo is a convenient pre-arrival option.

cultural.tipping: Not obligatory but appreciated. Leave 5-10% at restaurants for good service (service is not automatically included). Cafes: leave small coins. Taxi drivers: round up. Portugal has lower tipping expectations than Spain or France.
cultural.dressCode: Casual to smart casual. Cover up for churches (shoulders and knees). Lisbon and Porto are fashionable cities but not snobbish about dress. Practical clothing for hills (Lisbon is famously hilly — comfortable shoes essential).
cultural.greetings: Handshake on first meeting. Friends exchange two cheek kisses (right first). Very warm and welcoming — Portuguese are known for saudade (a melancholic warmth). 'Bom dia/Boa tarde/Boa noite' always appreciated.
taboos: Confusing Portugal with Spain (or assuming it's similar) — culturally distinct
Assuming everyone speaks Spanish (Portuguese is different — they speak Portuguese)
Not acknowledging saudade — the Portuguese are proud of this cultural concept
Speaking too loudly (Portuguese culture values modesty and discretion)
Rushing through a pastel de nata — these must be savored
Leaving food on your plate at someone's home (seen as insulting the cook)
cultural.haggling: Not practiced in shops or restaurants. Some flexibility at antique markets and flea markets (Feira da Ladra in Lisbon).

safety.lgbtSafety: Very LGBTQ+ friendly. Same-sex marriage legal since 2010. Lisbon and Porto have active LGBTQ+ scenes. Lisbon Pride is one of Europe's largest. Very welcoming overall.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Very safe. One of Europe's safest countries for solo female travelers.
safety.notes: Portugal consistently ranks among Europe's safest countries. Petty crime (pickpocketing) is the main concern in Lisbon's tourist areas (Alfama, Baixa, Bairro Alto nightlife). Standard vigilance in crowded areas. Wildfires are a risk in rural areas in summer.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen zone). UK citizens: 90 days in any 180-day period.
practical.timeZone: UTC+00:00 (WET) / UTC+01:00 (WEST in summer) — same as UK/Ireland
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-October for warm, sunny weather. June-August is peak season and crowded. May and September offer ideal weather with fewer tourists. Madeira and Azores are worth visiting year-round.

hospitals.name: Hospital de Santa Maria
hospitals.notes: Main public hospital in Lisbon. EU citizens treated under EHIC. Some English-speaking doctors.

hospitals.name: Hospital de São João
hospitals.notes: Major university hospital in Porto. Good emergency services.

immediate: Follow ANEPC (emergency authority) and municipal alerts immediately
Evacuate when ordered — Portuguese wildfires can move faster than walking pace
Drive with headlights on in smoky conditions
after: Avoid burned areas — unstable trees and toxic ash

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 112)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (112) and ambulance (112) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
